concepts.def: The narrowest blood vessel, with a wall only one endothelial cell thick and a lumen so narrow that red blood cells pass through in single file. Capillaries branch repeatedly to form networks that penetrate every tissue, giving a very large total surface area for exchange of materials between the blood and the internal or external environment.

A pore through the endothelial cell of a capillary wall, found in capillaries where exchange needs to be particularly rapid, such as those of the kidney glomerulus and the villi of the small intestine. Fenestrations allow water and small solutes to pass out of the plasma quickly but are far too small for blood cells to leave the vessel.

The central space of a blood vessel through which the blood flows. In a micrograph the thickness of the vessel wall compared with the diameter of the lumen distinguishes an artery (thick wall, narrow round lumen) from a vein (thin wall, wide and often irregular lumen).

A vessel that carries blood away from the heart. Its wall is thick relative to the lumen and contains layers of smooth muscle and elastic tissue, surrounded by an outer layer of collagen, so it can withstand and maintain the high, pulsing pressure of blood leaving the heart.

A vessel that carries blood back towards the heart at low pressure. Its wall is thin relative to its wide lumen, with only a little muscle and elastic tissue, and it contains valves that prevent backflow of blood.

concepts.term: Elastic tissue of the artery wall
concepts.def: Tissue containing elastic fibres in the wall of an artery. It stretches when the ventricle contracts and blood is forced in at high pressure, then recoils as the ventricle relaxes, so pressure is maintained and blood keeps flowing between heartbeats rather than falling to zero.

concepts.term: Smooth muscle of the artery wall
concepts.def: The layer of muscle in the artery wall that, together with the elastic tissue, helps the artery withstand high pressure. Contraction of the muscle narrows the lumen (vasoconstriction) and relaxation widens it (vasodilation), which helps to maintain and regulate blood pressure and to control how much blood flows to a tissue. The muscle does not pump the blood along; the heart does that.

The wave of pressure that passes along the wall of an artery each time the left ventricle contracts and forces blood into the aorta. It can be felt with the fingertips where an artery lies close to the skin, such as the radial artery in the wrist or the carotid artery in the neck, so counting the pulse for a known time gives the heart rate in beats per minute.

A pocket-shaped flap of tissue in the wall of a vein that opens when blood moves towards the heart and closes when blood starts to move backwards, so blood can flow in one direction only. Valves are needed because blood pressure in veins is too low to prevent backflow on its own.

One of the arteries that branch from the aorta just above the aortic valve and run over the surface of the heart, supplying the cardiac muscle itself with oxygenated blood. Blood in the chambers of the heart does not supply the heart wall; the coronary vessels do.

Blockage of a coronary artery, usually when fatty deposits (atheroma) build up in the artery wall and narrow the lumen, and a blood clot then forms at the damaged site and blocks it completely. The cardiac muscle beyond the blockage is deprived of oxygen and dies, which is a myocardial infarction (heart attack).

A number between -1 and +1 that quantifies how strongly two variables are related. The sign shows the direction of the relationship (positive when both rise together, negative when one rises as the other falls) and the size shows its strength, with values near zero showing little or no correlation. Even a strong correlation, such as that between saturated fat intake and coronary heart disease, does not prove that one variable causes the other.

The loss of water vapour from a plant, mainly through the stomata of the leaves. Water evaporates from the wet cellulose cell walls of mesophyll cells into the air spaces of the leaf and the vapour then diffuses out through open stomata.

The negative pressure potential generated in the xylem when water evaporates from leaf cell walls. Water is drawn out of the xylem vessels and through the cell walls by capillary action to replace what is lost, putting the whole column of water in the xylem under tension, and it is this tension that draws water up from the roots to the leaves.

The attraction between water molecules due to hydrogen bonding. Because water molecules hold on to one another, the column of water in a xylem vessel stays continuous when it is pulled upwards under tension instead of breaking apart.

The movement of water through narrow spaces, such as the gaps between cellulose fibres in a cell wall, driven by adhesion of water to the surfaces and cohesion between water molecules. In the leaf it draws water out of the xylem and through the cell walls towards the sites of evaporation.

A continuous tube for transport of water formed from a column of cells that have died and lost their cell contents. The end walls between the cells are incomplete or absent, so water flows through unimpeded, and the side walls are thickened with lignin.

A hard, waterproof polymer deposited in the walls of xylem vessels. Lignified walls are strong enough to withstand the tension in the water column without the vessel collapsing inwards, and they also help support the plant.

A gap in the lignified wall of a xylem vessel where only the thin primary cell wall remains. Pits allow water to enter the vessel from the root cortex and to leave it into surrounding cells and neighbouring vessels in the stem and leaf.

A strand of vascular tissue containing xylem and phloem. In a transverse section of a dicotyledonous stem the vascular bundles are arranged in a ring near the outside, with the xylem on the inner side of each bundle and the phloem on the outer side.

The region of unspecialized parenchyma cells that lies between the epidermis and the vascular tissue in both stems and roots. It is a storage and packing tissue, not a transport tissue; in a stem the outer cortex cells may also contain chloroplasts and photosynthesize.

The single outer layer of cells covering a stem or root. In a stem it is covered by a waxy cuticle that reduces water loss and protects against pathogens; in a root it lacks a cuticle and bears root hairs that absorb water and mineral ions.

The central core of vascular tissue in a transverse section of a dicotyledonous root. The xylem forms a star or cross shape at the centre and the phloem lies in separate groups between the arms of the xylem, all surrounded by the cortex and the epidermis. This differs from the ring of separate vascular bundles seen in a stem.

The fluid that bathes the cells of a tissue. It is formed by pressure filtration of plasma through the capillary wall and has the same composition as plasma except that it contains almost no plasma proteins and no blood cells. Cells exchange substances with tissue fluid, not directly with the blood.

The formation of tissue fluid when the hydrostatic pressure of blood at the arteriole end of a capillary forces water and small solutes out through gaps and fenestrations in the capillary wall, leaving plasma proteins and cells behind. At the venule end the blood pressure is lower, so tissue fluid drains back into the capillary.

The liquid part of blood, in which the cells are suspended. It is mostly water with dissolved glucose, amino acids, mineral ions, dissolved gases, urea, hormones and plasma proteins such as albumin. Tissue fluid is plasma minus most of the plasma proteins.

Excess tissue fluid that has drained into lymph ducts rather than back into the capillaries. Lymph ducts have thin walls with gaps through which tissue fluid enters and valves that prevent backflow, and the lymph is returned to the blood circulation through ducts that empty into veins near the heart.

The circulation of a bony fish, in which blood passes through the heart once in each complete circuit: heart to gills, where it is oxygenated, then directly on to the rest of the body and back to the heart. Pressure lost in the gill capillaries is not restored, so blood reaches the body tissues at low pressure.

The circulation of a mammal, in which blood passes through the heart twice in each complete circuit. The right side of the heart pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs (pulmonary circulation) and the blood returns to the left side, which pumps it at high pressure to the rest of the body (systemic circulation).

The specialized muscle of the heart wall. Its cells are branched and joined so that the electrical signal for contraction spreads rapidly from cell to cell, and it contracts rhythmically without fatigue for a lifetime. The thickness of cardiac muscle in each chamber matches the pressure that chamber must generate.

A group of specialized cardiac muscle cells in the wall of the right atrium that initiates each heartbeat by generating an electrical impulse without any signal from the nervous system. The impulse spreads across the atria, then to the ventricles, so contraction is coordinated.

The valves between each atrium and its ventricle. They are pushed open when atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure, so blood flows into the ventricles, and are forced shut when the ventricles contract and their pressure rises above that of the atria, preventing backflow into the atria.

The valves at the exit of each ventricle, at the base of the aorta and of the pulmonary artery. They open when ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure during ventricular contraction and close when the ventricles relax, preventing blood in the arteries from flowing back into the heart.

The wall of cardiac muscle that separates the right and left sides of the heart, so that deoxygenated blood on the right side cannot mix with oxygenated blood on the left side and the two circulations are kept at different pressures.

Systole is the phase of the cardiac cycle in which a chamber of the heart contracts; diastole is the phase in which it relaxes and fills. Atrial systole is followed by ventricular systole, and then all chambers are in diastole together while blood flows in from the veins.

The two values in a blood pressure reading such as 120/80 mm Hg, both measured in an artery. Systolic pressure is the peak arterial pressure reached during ventricular systole; diastolic pressure is the minimum arterial pressure during ventricular diastole, which remains well above zero because of elastic recoil of the artery walls.

A positive pressure potential generated in the xylem of the root. Cells around the xylem actively transport mineral ions into the xylem, lowering its water potential so that water follows by osmosis, and the accumulating water pushes upwards. It moves water when transpiration is insufficient, for example in high humidity or in spring before the leaves of deciduous plants have opened.

A living phloem cell that forms part of a sieve tube. It has no nucleus and only a thin layer of cytoplasm with few organelles, so the sap can flow through it with little resistance, and its end walls are perforated sieve plates through which sap passes to the next element.

A phloem cell next to each sieve tube element, with a nucleus, dense cytoplasm and many mitochondria. It carries out the metabolic functions the sieve tube element cannot, and uses ATP from its mitochondria to load carbon compounds such as sucrose into the sieve tube at sources and to unload them at sinks.
Channels of cytoplasm passing through the cell walls between a companion cell and its sieve tube element, through which sugars and other substances move from one cell to the other.

A source is a part of the plant that loads carbon compounds into the phloem, such as a photosynthesizing leaf or a storage organ releasing its reserves; a sink is a part that unloads and uses or stores them, such as a growing root, a fruit or a developing bud. Phloem sap flows from source to sink, in whichever direction that lies.

The two thin-walled upper chambers of the heart that collect blood returning in veins: the right atrium from the venae cavae and the left atrium from the pulmonary veins. Because the atria only have to push blood a short distance through the open atrioventricular valves into the ventricles directly below, their walls contain little cardiac muscle; atrial contraction completes the filling of the ventricles before ventricular systole begins.

mcqs.q: Why is the wall of a capillary only one cell thick?
options: It keeps the distance over which substances diffuse between blood and tissue cells very short.
It lets blood pass through the capillary faster, so that more blood reaches the tissue cells.
It leaves room for a lumen wide enough for red blood cells to pass through side by side.
It allows red blood cells to squeeze out through the wall and into the tissues.
mcqs.specStatementText: Capillaries are built for exchange
mcqs.explain: Exchange across the capillary wall is by diffusion, and the rate of diffusion falls steeply as distance increases. A wall of a single endothelial cell keeps that distance to a minimum, so exchange is rapid.
rationales: Exchange across the capillary wall is by diffusion, and the rate of diffusion falls steeply as distance increases. A wall of a single endothelial cell keeps that distance to a minimum, so exchange is rapid.

A student who thinks a thin wall is an easy-flow pipe picks this. In fact blood flows more slowly in capillaries than in any other vessel; the thin wall shortens the diffusion distance, it does not speed the flow.

A student who believes a wider vessel is better for exchange picks this. In fact capillaries are narrow, with red blood cells passing in single file, which is what brings every cell close to the wall.

A student who pictures capillaries as full of large holes picks this. Red blood cells stay inside the capillary; the thin wall is about diffusion distance, and the fenestrations found in some capillaries are pores far too small for cells.

mcqs.q: A muscle receives blood through a network of thousands of capillaries rather than through a single vessel of the same total volume. What is the advantage of this arrangement for exchange?
options: A single wide vessel would have more wall area than thousands of narrow ones, so exchange inside it would be faster.
The total surface area of the many narrow, branching vessels is far larger, and all the blood is close to a wall.
The narrow capillaries force the blood through faster, so more oxygen is delivered to the muscle each second.
Each capillary has fenestrations, which are needed so that cells can pass out of the blood into the muscle.
mcqs.specStatementText: Capillaries are built for exchange
mcqs.explain: Branching and narrow diameters are the adaptations the guide names for surface area. Dividing the blood among many narrow tubes multiplies the wall area available for exchange and ensures no part of the blood is more than a few micrometres from the wall.
rationales: A student who compares one wide vessel with one narrow vessel picks this. Summed over the network, the thousands of narrow capillaries have a far larger total wall area and a far higher surface area to volume ratio.

Branching and narrow diameters are the adaptations the guide names for surface area. Dividing the blood among many narrow tubes multiplies the wall area available for exchange and ensures no part of the blood is more than a few micrometres from the wall.
A student who thinks capillary design is about speed of flow picks this. Flow is actually slowest in capillaries, which gives more time for exchange; the advantage is surface area, not speed.

A student who believes all capillaries are fenestrated and that fenestrations pass cells picks this. Muscle capillaries are continuous, without fenestrations, and fenestrations do not pass cells in any case.

mcqs.q: A micrograph shows two blood vessels in transverse section. Vessel X has a wall about as thick as the diameter of its small, round lumen. Vessel Y has a wall that is very thin compared with its wide, irregular lumen. Which identification is correct?
options: Y is an artery, because its wide lumen carries the large volume of blood that is at high pressure.
X is a vein, because a vein needs a thick muscular wall to pump blood back towards the heart.
X is an artery, because its wall is thick relative to its lumen to withstand high pressure.
Neither can be identified, because a micrograph cannot show whether blood is oxygenated.
mcqs.specStatementText: Telling arteries from veins in a micrograph
mcqs.explain: The guide's criterion is the thickness of the wall relative to the diameter of the lumen. A thick muscular and elastic wall around a narrow, round lumen is the section of an artery; the thin wall and collapsed, wide lumen of Y are typical of a vein.
rationales: A student who expects the high-pressure vessel to be the wider one picks this. An artery has a thick wall relative to its lumen; the thin-walled, wide, irregular vessel Y is a vein.
A student who thinks veins have thick muscular walls that pump blood back picks this. Vein walls are thin and rely on compression by surrounding muscle, so the thick-walled vessel X is the artery.

The guide's criterion is the thickness of the wall relative to the diameter of the lumen. A thick muscular and elastic wall around a narrow, round lumen is the section of an artery; the thin wall and collapsed, wide lumen of Y are typical of a vein.

A student who defines arteries by the oxygen content of their blood picks this. Vessels are identified in section by wall structure and wall thickness relative to the lumen, not by oxygenation, so X is the artery and Y the vein.

mcqs.q: What is the role of the elastic tissue in the wall of an artery?
options: It contracts in waves behind the blood to push it along the artery towards the tissues.
It makes the wall stiff and rigid so that the high pressure cannot burst the artery.
It forms flaps that actively open and shut to push blood forwards along the artery.
It stretches during systole and recoils during diastole, maintaining pressure.
mcqs.specStatementText: How arteries handle high pressure
mcqs.explain: The layers of muscle and elastic tissue allow the artery to withstand and maintain high pressure. Stretching during ventricular contraction stores energy that the recoil returns during relaxation, keeping blood moving and pressure high between beats.
rationales: A student who thinks the artery wall pumps like the gut wall picks this. Elastic tissue is not muscle and generates no propulsive wave; the heart provides the force that moves blood.

A student who equates a strong wall with a rigid wall picks this. A rigid artery would let pressure fall to zero between beats; elastic tissue is there precisely because the wall must stretch and recoil.

A student who gives valves an active pushing role picks this. Elastic tissue is not valve tissue and no valve, venous or cardiac, generates force; the artery's elastic tissue stretches and recoils to maintain pressure (B3.2.3).

The layers of muscle and elastic tissue allow the artery to withstand and maintain high pressure. Stretching during ventricular contraction stores energy that the recoil returns during relaxation, keeping blood moving and pressure high between beats.

mcqs.q: The pulmonary artery carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. Which statement about this vessel is correct?
options: It is an artery because it carries blood away from the heart, whatever the oxygen content.
It carries oxygenated blood, because by definition every artery carries oxygenated blood.
Its wall is thick and rigid so that pressure from the right ventricle cannot burst it.
Its muscular wall contracts to pump the deoxygenated blood along to the lungs.
mcqs.specStatementText: How arteries handle high pressure
mcqs.explain: Arteries are adapted for transporting blood away from the heart, whatever the oxygen content of that blood. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs and has the thick, elastic wall of an artery.
rationales: Arteries are adapted for transporting blood away from the heart, whatever the oxygen content of that blood. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs and has the thick, elastic wall of an artery.

A student who has turned the red-and-blue diagram convention into a definition picks this. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood; arteries are defined by direction of flow, not oxygen content.
A student who equates a strong wall with a rigid wall picks this. The pulmonary artery, like every artery, has an elastic wall that stretches and recoils to maintain pressure between beats (B3.2.3).
A student who thinks artery walls pump picks this. The right ventricle provides the force; the muscle and elastic tissue of the wall withstand the pressure and regulate the diameter.

mcqs.q: A student counts 12 beats in 10 seconds at the radial pulse. Immediately afterwards a digital heart rate monitor on the same person reads 74 beats per minute. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: The fingertip method gives 72 beats per minute but cannot be compared with the monitor, because it measures blood flow rather than heart rate.
The values agree within the error of a 10-second count, about 6 beats per minute; a 60-second count would allow a fairer comparison.
The fingertip count of exactly 72 beats per minute is precise, so the digital monitor must be reading 2 beats per minute too high.
The student must have counted at a vein instead of an artery, which gives a slightly lower reading than the monitor does.
mcqs.specStatementText: Taking a pulse
mcqs.explain: 12 beats in 10 s gives 12 x 6 = 72 beats per minute. A miscount of one beat in 10 s is scaled to 6 beats per minute, so 72 and 74 are consistent. Counting for a full minute reduces this error and makes the traditional and digital methods comparable.
rationales: A student who thinks the pulse is the blood flowing past picks this. The pulse is a pressure wave produced by each ventricular contraction, so pulse rate and heart rate are the same quantity and can be compared directly.

12 beats in 10 s gives 12 x 6 = 72 beats per minute. A miscount of one beat in 10 s is scaled to 6 beats per minute, so 72 and 74 are consistent. Counting for a full minute reduces this error and makes the traditional and digital methods comparable.

A student who trusts the multiplied count as exact picks this. Any miscount of one beat in 10 s is multiplied by 6, so the fingertip value carries an uncertainty of about 6 beats per minute and the monitor is not shown to be faulty.
A student who thinks a pulse can be felt in a vein picks this. No pulse exists in veins, so a vein could not have given a count at all; the small difference is explained by counting error.

mcqs.q: Why can heart rate be determined by feeling the carotid or radial pulse with the fingertips?
options: Because blood is pushed past the fingertips in one surge each time the muscular artery wall contracts.
Because the blood flowing through the artery can be felt as it moves past the fingertips.
Because a pressure wave passes along the artery wall each time the left ventricle contracts.
Because these are the places where large veins close to the surface of the skin carry the heartbeat.
mcqs.specStatementText: Taking a pulse
mcqs.explain: Each ventricular contraction forces blood into the aorta and sends a pressure wave along the arteries. Where an artery lies close to the skin, such as the carotid or radial artery, the fingertips feel the wall expanding once per heartbeat, so counting pulses gives the heart rate.
rationales: A student who thinks the artery wall pumps picks this. The artery does not contract to push each surge; it is stretched by the pressure wave from the ventricle.
A student who thinks the pulse is the movement of blood picks this. Blood flows continuously; what is felt is the intermittent pressure wave that stretches the wall.

Each ventricular contraction forces blood into the aorta and sends a pressure wave along the arteries. Where an artery lies close to the skin, such as the carotid or radial artery, the fingertips feel the wall expanding once per heartbeat, so counting pulses gives the heart rate.
A student who thinks the pulse is found in veins picks this. The carotid and radial pulses are arterial; the pressure wave has been lost by the time blood reaches the veins.

mcqs.q: Which combination of features adapts a vein for returning blood to the heart at low pressure?
options: A thick layer of muscle that contracts rhythmically, and a narrow lumen that keeps the pressure high.
Valves that open and shut actively to push blood along, and a wall of elastic tissue that recoils.
A pulse that travels along the wall and squeezes blood forwards, and a thick wall to resist it.
Valves that prevent backflow, and a flexible wall compressed by surrounding muscle.
mcqs.specStatementText: How veins get blood back
mcqs.explain: These are the adaptations the guide names. Skeletal muscles around a vein squeeze its flexible wall, pushing blood along, and the pocket valves close whenever blood begins to move backwards, so the net movement is towards the heart.
rationales: A student who models veins on arteries picks this. Veins have thin walls with little muscle and a wide lumen; the pressure in them is low and they are not self-pumping.
A student who gives the valves an active role picks this. Venous valves are passive flaps that only prevent backflow, and veins have little elastic tissue.
A student who thinks veins carry a pulse picks this. The pressure wave has been damped out by the capillaries; there is no pulse in veins and no thick wall.

These are the adaptations the guide names. Skeletal muscles around a vein squeeze its flexible wall, pushing blood along, and the pocket valves close whenever blood begins to move backwards, so the net movement is towards the heart.

mcqs.q: A soldier standing motionless on parade for a long time feels faint, but the feeling passes as soon as she flexes her leg muscles. What is the best explanation?
options: Standing still removes the muscle contractions that squeeze the leg veins, so less blood returns to the heart until she moves.
Standing still tires the muscular walls of the leg veins, so they can no longer contract to pump blood up to the heart.
Standing still stops the valves in the leg veins from opening and shutting, so they no longer push blood up to the heart.
Standing still stops the artery walls from contracting, so blood can no longer be pumped from the heart to the brain.
mcqs.specStatementText: How veins get blood back
mcqs.explain: Return of blood through veins depends on their flexible walls being compressed by surrounding muscle action, with valves preventing backflow. Without movement, blood pools in the leg veins, less returns to the heart, and blood supply to the brain falls. Flexing the muscles squeezes the veins and restores venous return.
rationales: Return of blood through veins depends on their flexible walls being compressed by surrounding muscle action, with valves preventing backflow. Without movement, blood pools in the leg veins, less returns to the heart, and blood supply to the brain falls. Flexing the muscles squeezes the veins and restores venous return.
A student who thinks veins pump with their own muscular walls picks this. Vein walls are thin and are not what propels blood; it is the surrounding skeletal muscles that must contract.
A student who thinks the valves drive the flow picks this. Valves are passive and only prevent backflow; they cannot push blood, so the loss of muscle compression is the real cause.
A student who thinks artery walls pump picks this. Arteries never pump, and the heart continues to beat; the problem is reduced return of blood to the heart through the veins.

mcqs.q: A blood clot completely occludes a branch of a coronary artery. What is the direct consequence?
options: Blood can no longer pass through the chambers of the heart, so the heart stops beating almost at once.
The region of cardiac muscle supplied by that branch is deprived of oxygen and its cells die.
Fat from the diet keeps building up on the surface of the clot until the artery bursts open.
The muscle in the artery wall contracts to force the clot along, tearing the artery wall.
mcqs.specStatementText: Blocked coronary arteries, and what correlations can prove
mcqs.explain: The coronary arteries supply the cardiac muscle of the heart wall. Occlusion cuts off the oxygen supply to the muscle beyond the block, so the cells there die: a myocardial infarction. The damaged region may then fail to contract properly.
rationales: A student who thinks the coronary arteries are the route blood takes through the heart picks this. Blood continues to flow through the chambers; it is the muscle of the wall that loses its supply.

The coronary arteries supply the cardiac muscle of the heart wall. Occlusion cuts off the oxygen supply to the muscle beyond the block, so the cells there die: a myocardial infarction. The damaged region may then fail to contract properly.
A student who holds the grease-in-a-drainpipe model picks this. Atheroma forms within the artery wall, and the consequence of occlusion is oxygen starvation of muscle, not bursting.
A student who thinks artery walls pump picks this. Artery muscle does not push contents along; the harm done by occlusion is to the cardiac muscle downstream.

mcqs.q: In a study of 20 countries, the correlation coefficient between mean saturated fat intake and the death rate from coronary heart disease was +0.85. What can be concluded from this result alone?
options: Saturated fat in the diet is shown to cause coronary heart disease, because the coefficient is so close to +1, the maximum.
The relationship is weak, because a correlation calculated from only 20 countries cannot be a strong one.
There is a strong positive correlation between the variables, but this does not prove that one causes the other.
Saturated fat from food coats the inside of the coronary arteries, which is why the two variables rise together in step.
mcqs.specStatementText: Blocked coronary arteries, and what correlations can prove
mcqs.explain: A coefficient of +0.85 quantifies a strong positive relationship: countries with higher fat intake tend to have higher death rates. Correlation coefficients assess the strength of a relationship, but a causal link can only be established with other evidence, since confounding variables may be responsible.
rationales: A student who treats a strong correlation as proof of cause picks this. The guide is explicit that even the strong correlation between saturated fat intake and coronary heart disease does not prove a causal link; other factors could vary alongside fat intake.

A student who takes sample size as the measure of strength picks this. The strength of the relationship is given by the coefficient itself; +0.85 is a strong positive correlation. A small sample lowers confidence in the value, which is a separate question (B3.2.6 NOS).

A coefficient of +0.85 quantifies a strong positive relationship: countries with higher fat intake tend to have higher death rates. Correlation coefficients assess the strength of a relationship, but a causal link can only be established with other evidence, since confounding variables may be responsible.

A student who thinks dietary fat lines the artery like grease in a pipe, and who reads a mechanism into a correlation, picks this. The data give no mechanism, and atheroma forms within the artery wall rather than as fat coating the lumen.

mcqs.q: Researchers calculated correlation coefficients between the incidence of coronary heart disease and four factors: smoking (2000 people) +0.72, hours of exercise per week (500 people) -0.65, dietary fibre intake (3000 people) +0.08, and blood cholesterol (400 people) +0.61. Which factor shows the weakest relationship with coronary heart disease?
options: Hours of exercise per week, because a negative coefficient shows a weaker relationship than any positive one.
Blood cholesterol, because it was measured in the fewest people, so its relationship is the weakest.
Smoking, because even a strong correlation of +0.72 cannot prove that smoking causes the disease.
Dietary fibre intake, because +0.08 is closest to zero, showing little or no correlation.
mcqs.specStatementText: Blocked coronary arteries, and what correlations can prove
mcqs.explain: The size of a correlation coefficient, ignoring its sign, measures the strength of the relationship. +0.08 is very close to zero, so fibre intake shows almost no correlation with the disease in these data; such a low coefficient could count as evidence against a hypothesis that fibre affects coronary heart disease.
rationales: A student who reads a negative sign as meaning a weak relationship picks this. -0.65 is a strong negative correlation: more exercise is associated with less disease. The sign gives direction, not strength.

A student who confuses the reliability of a study with the strength of a correlation picks this. Sample size affects how much confidence to place in a coefficient, but the strength of the relationship is given by the coefficient itself; +0.61 is a moderately strong correlation.
A student who confuses the question of causation with the question of strength picks this. Whether or not it proves cause, +0.72 is the strongest relationship in the list, not the weakest.

The size of a correlation coefficient, ignoring its sign, measures the strength of the relationship. +0.08 is very close to zero, so fibre intake shows almost no correlation with the disease in these data; such a low coefficient could count as evidence against a hypothesis that fibre affects coronary heart disease.

mcqs.q: What generates the force that draws water up the xylem from the roots to the leaves?
options: Evaporation of water from leaf cell walls draws water out of the xylem, putting the water column under tension.
Cells in the root pump water into the base of the xylem, pushing the whole column up to the leaves.
The living xylem cells use ATP from respiration to move water molecules upwards against gravity.
Water evaporates from the open ends of the xylem vessels at the leaf surface, sucking the column up.
mcqs.specStatementText: Water is pulled up the xylem, not pushed
mcqs.explain: Loss of water by transpiration from the cell walls of leaf cells causes water to be drawn out of the xylem vessels and through cell walls by capillary action. This generates tension, a negative pressure potential, and it is this tension that draws water up the xylem.
rationales: Loss of water by transpiration from the cell walls of leaf cells causes water to be drawn out of the xylem vessels and through cell walls by capillary action. This generates tension, a negative pressure potential, and it is this tension that draws water up the xylem.

A student who locates the force at the bottom, like a pump, picks this. Root pressure is too small to lift water up a tall plant; the water is pulled from above by the tension that transpiration generates.
A student who assumes uphill movement needs cellular energy picks this. Xylem vessels are dead and have no cell contents; the energy comes from the sun evaporating water in the leaf.

A student who thinks evaporation happens straight from the xylem picks this. Xylem vessels do not open at the leaf surface; water leaves them through pits, moves through the cell walls of leaf cells, and evaporates from those walls into the air spaces.

mcqs.q: In a tall tree the column of water in the xylem is under considerable tension, yet it does not break into separate lengths with gaps between them. Which property of water explains this?
options: Water molecules are attracted to the lignin of the vessel wall, which holds each part of the column in place.
Water molecules are held to one another by hydrogen bonds, so the whole column moves as an unbroken unit.
Water is pushed steadily upwards from the roots, so the column is kept under compression, not tension.
Water molecules are pulled upwards by active transport in the xylem, faster than any gaps could form.
mcqs.specStatementText: Water is pulled up the xylem, not pushed
mcqs.explain: This is cohesion. Hydrogen bonding between water molecules means that when the topmost molecules are drawn out into leaf cell walls, they pull the molecules below with them, so a continuous column is maintained under tension all the way from the roots.
rationales: A student who assigns the column-holding role to sticking to walls picks this. Adhesion to walls does not stop the column snapping in the middle; it is the attraction of water molecules to each other that keeps it continuous.

This is cohesion. Hydrogen bonding between water molecules means that when the topmost molecules are drawn out into leaf cell walls, they pull the molecules below with them, so a continuous column is maintained under tension all the way from the roots.

A student who thinks water is pushed from below picks this. The column in a transpiring plant is under tension, not compression, as the stem's shrinking diameter during the day shows; a push would not explain why it holds together.
A student who expects a cellular energy input picks this. Xylem vessels have no cell contents and carry out no active transport; the continuity of the column is a physical property of water.

mcqs.q: Why are the walls of xylem vessels thickened with lignin?
options: To seal the vessel completely so that no water can escape through the side walls into surrounding cells.
To provide the mitochondria and cytoplasm of the vessel with a surface on which to generate ATP for transport.
To withstand the tension in the water column so that the vessel is not pulled inwards and collapsed.
To hold the plant upright, which is the only function that lignin has anywhere in the xylem.
mcqs.specStatementText: Xylem vessels are built for flow under tension
mcqs.explain: The negative pressure potential generated by transpiration would suck a soft-walled tube flat. Lignified walls are rigid enough to withstand these tensions, keeping the vessel open for unimpeded flow; they also contribute to supporting the plant.
rationales: A student who pictures a sealed pipe picks this. Lignified walls contain many pits through which water enters and leaves the vessel; sealing the wall would prevent water reaching leaf cells.
A student who assumes xylem transport is active picks this. Mature xylem vessels have no cytoplasm or mitochondria; they are empty tubes and transport is passive.

The negative pressure potential generated by transpiration would suck a soft-walled tube flat. Lignified walls are rigid enough to withstand these tensions, keeping the vessel open for unimpeded flow; they also contribute to supporting the plant.
A student who remembers lignin only as the support material picks this. Support is a role, but for transport the essential function is resisting the tension that would otherwise collapse the vessel.

mcqs.q: A xylem vessel in a leaf vein is blocked by an air bubble. Water still reaches the leaf cells beyond the blockage. Which feature of xylem makes this possible?
options: Living xylem cells actively transport water around the blockage using ATP from respiration.
The lignified side walls are completely sealed, so water can only move through the open ends.
The end walls of the vessel are absent, so water is pushed past the bubble from below.
Pits in the lignified walls let water pass sideways into a neighbouring vessel.
mcqs.specStatementText: Xylem vessels are built for flow under tension
mcqs.explain: Pits are gaps in the lignified wall for entry and exit of water. Water below the bubble can pass through pits into an adjacent vessel, bypass the blockage, and re-enter or continue on to the leaf cells, so a single blocked vessel does not stop supply.
rationales: A student who expects the xylem to solve the problem by active transport picks this. Xylem vessels are dead, with no cell contents, and cannot carry out active transport.
A student who thinks lignin seals the vessel picks this. If the side walls were sealed, a blocked vessel would cut off everything beyond it; it is the openings in the walls that allow a bypass.

A student who imagines water being pushed from below picks this. Missing end walls give unimpeded flow along one vessel, but they cannot get water past a bubble in that vessel; water must leave sideways.

Pits are gaps in the lignified wall for entry and exit of water. Water below the bubble can pass through pits into an adjacent vessel, bypass the blockage, and re-enter or continue on to the leaf cells, so a single blocked vessel does not stop supply.

mcqs.q: A student is drawing a plan diagram from a micrograph of a transverse section of a dicotyledonous stem. Which description matches what should be drawn?
options: A ring of vascular bundles near the outside, each with xylem towards the centre and phloem towards the epidermis, and cortex outside the ring.
A single central mass of vascular tissue, with xylem forming a star and phloem between its arms, surrounded by a wide cortex.
A ring of vascular bundles near the outside, each with phloem towards the centre and xylem towards the epidermis, and pith in the middle.
A wide cortex carrying water and sugars up the stem, with a thin ring of xylem and phloem that provides support only.
mcqs.specStatementText: Tissues in a stem section
mcqs.explain: In a dicotyledonous stem the vascular bundles are arranged in a ring. Within each bundle the xylem lies on the inner side and the phloem on the outer side; the cortex lies between the ring and the single-layered epidermis, and pith fills the centre.
rationales: In a dicotyledonous stem the vascular bundles are arranged in a ring. Within each bundle the xylem lies on the inner side and the phloem on the outer side; the cortex lies between the ring and the single-layered epidermis, and pith fills the centre.
A student who expects transport tissue to run down the middle picks this. A central star of xylem is the arrangement in a root; a stem has a ring of separate vascular bundles.
A student who has reversed the two tissues within the bundle picks this. Xylem is on the inner side of each bundle, towards the centre; phloem is on the outer side.
A student who thinks the cortex is a transport tissue picks this. The cortex is storage and packing tissue; xylem and phloem in the vascular bundles carry out transport.

mcqs.q: In a transverse section of a dicotyledonous root, where are the xylem and the phloem found?
options: In separate vascular bundles arranged in a ring near the outside of the root, in just the same way as in the stem.
At the centre of the root, with the xylem forming a star shape and groups of phloem between its arms.
At the centre of the root, with phloem forming a star shape and xylem in groups between its arms.
Spread throughout the cortex, which conducts water and sugars across the width of the root.
mcqs.specStatementText: Tissues in a root section
mcqs.explain: The dicotyledonous root has a central vascular cylinder: xylem forms a star or cross shape in the middle and phloem lies in separate groups between the arms of the xylem. This is surrounded by the cortex and then the epidermis bearing root hairs.
rationales: A student who applies the stem pattern to the root picks this. A root has no ring of separate bundles; its vascular tissue is grouped in a central cylinder.

The dicotyledonous root has a central vascular cylinder: xylem forms a star or cross shape in the middle and phloem lies in separate groups between the arms of the xylem. This is surrounded by the cortex and then the epidermis bearing root hairs.
A student who has swapped the two tissues picks this. It is the xylem that forms the central star in a root, with phloem between the arms.

A student who thinks the cortex is a transport tissue picks this. Water does cross the cortex to reach the xylem, but the cortex is parenchyma for storage and packing; xylem and phloem are confined to the centre.

mcqs.q: Blood pressure in a capillary is about 4.7 kPa at the arteriole end and about 1.3 kPa at the venule end. How do these values explain the release and reuptake of tissue fluid?
options: Plasma diffuses out at the arteriole end because its concentration is higher there, and diffuses back in at the venule end where it is lower.
The pressure at the two ends is effectively the same, so fluid must be pumped back into the capillary by the venule.
At 4.7 kPa the pressure forces fluid out through the capillary wall; at 1.3 kPa it cannot, so tissue fluid drains back in.
The higher pressure at the arteriole end forces out blood cells and plasma proteins, which then return with the fluid at the venule end.
mcqs.specStatementText: Tissue fluid leaves and returns (HL)
mcqs.explain: Tissue fluid is formed by pressure filtration of plasma, promoted by the high pressure of blood arriving from arterioles. As blood flows along the capillary its pressure falls; at the venule end the lower pressure allows tissue fluid to drain back into the capillary.
rationales: A student who reaches for diffusion to explain every movement picks this. Plasma is not a solute with a concentration; tissue fluid is formed by pressure filtration, with fluid forced out through the capillary wall by hydrostatic pressure.

A student who assumes pressure is uniform along a vessel picks this. The values given differ by more than three times, and it is this fall in pressure, not a pump, that reverses the net movement of fluid.

Tissue fluid is formed by pressure filtration of plasma, promoted by the high pressure of blood arriving from arterioles. As blood flows along the capillary its pressure falls; at the venule end the lower pressure allows tissue fluid to drain back into the capillary.

A student who thinks filtration lets everything through picks this. Cells and almost all plasma proteins are too large to pass the capillary wall and stay in the blood; only water and small solutes leave.

mcqs.q: Samples of blood plasma and of tissue fluid from the same tissue were analysed. Both contained about 5 mmol per litre of glucose and similar concentrations of sodium ions, but plasma contained about 70 grams per litre of protein while tissue fluid contained only a small fraction of that amount. Which explanation of these results is correct?
options: Tissue fluid should have exactly the same composition as plasma, so the low protein value must be an error in the analysis.
The cells of the tissue took the protein directly from the blood inside the capillaries before the tissue fluid formed.
Glucose and ions diffused out of the capillary but proteins cannot diffuse, so tissue fluid formed by diffusion is protein-free.
Pressure filtration lets water and small solutes through the capillary wall but retains the large plasma proteins.
mcqs.specStatementText: Cells trade with tissue fluid, not blood (HL)
mcqs.explain: Glucose and sodium ions are small enough to pass through the gaps and fenestrations in the capillary wall along with the water, so their concentrations match. Plasma proteins such as albumin are too large to pass and stay in the plasma, which is the main difference in composition between plasma and tissue fluid.
rationales: A student who thinks tissue fluid is unchanged plasma picks this. The result is expected: plasma proteins are retained in the capillary because they are too large to be filtered out.

A student who thinks cells draw substances straight from the blood picks this. Cells exchange with tissue fluid, not directly with blood, and the missing protein never left the capillary in the first place.

A student who explains tissue fluid formation by diffusion picks this. Tissue fluid is formed by pressure filtration through gaps in the capillary wall; small solutes pass with the water while proteins are held back by their size.

Glucose and sodium ions are small enough to pass through the gaps and fenestrations in the capillary wall along with the water, so their concentrations match. Plasma proteins such as albumin are too large to pass and stay in the plasma, which is the main difference in composition between plasma and tissue fluid.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes how excess tissue fluid is drained and what happens to it?
options: It enters lymph ducts through gaps in their thin walls, valves prevent backflow, and the lymph is returned to the blood.
It enters lymph ducts, which pump it along with their thick muscular walls to the kidneys, where it is excreted.
It stays in the lymphatic system as lymph, a separate fluid that circulates without rejoining the blood.
It is pushed back into the capillaries by the valves in the lymph ducts, which force fluid towards the blood.
mcqs.specStatementText: Lymph drains the excess (HL)
mcqs.explain: Not all tissue fluid drains back into the capillaries. The excess enters lymph ducts, which have thin walls with gaps for entry and valves that keep the lymph moving one way, and the lymph ducts eventually empty into veins so the fluid rejoins the blood.
rationales: Not all tissue fluid drains back into the capillaries. The excess enters lymph ducts, which have thin walls with gaps for entry and valves that keep the lymph moving one way, and the lymph ducts eventually empty into veins so the fluid rejoins the blood.
A student who expects lymph ducts to be muscular pumps picks this. Lymph ducts have thin walls, are compressed by surrounding muscle, and return lymph to the blood, not to the kidneys.
A student who sees the lymphatic system as a closed circuit picks this. Lymph is returned to the blood circulation; if it were not, fluid would accumulate in the tissues.

A student who gives valves an active pushing role picks this. Valves are passive and only prevent backflow; lymph is moved by compression of the ducts and returned to the blood via veins, not pushed into capillaries.

mcqs.q: In a bony fish, mean blood pressure was measured at about 5 kPa in the artery leaving the heart and about 3.5 kPa in the vessel leaving the gills. In a mammal, mean pressure in the aorta was about 13 kPa. What do these data show about the two types of circulation?
options: Both circulations are double, because in each case the blood passes through two capillary beds, one for gas exchange and one for the rest of the body.
In the fish, blood loses pressure in the gill capillaries and goes on to the body at that lower pressure; in the mammal it is pumped again after the lungs.
The fish data must be unreliable, because blood leaves a capillary bed at the same pressure as it had when it entered, so the two fish values should be equal.
The mammalian value is higher because the muscular wall of the aorta contracts to pump blood onwards, adding to the pressure produced by the heart.
mcqs.specStatementText: Single and double circulation (HL)
mcqs.explain: The drop from 5 kPa to 3.5 kPa is the pressure lost in the gill capillaries, and in a single circulation this reduced-pressure blood goes straight on to the body without being pumped again. In the double circulation of a mammal, blood from the lungs returns to the left side of the heart and is pumped a second time, so the aorta carries blood at high pressure.
rationales: A student who counts capillary beds instead of passes through the heart picks this. The fish circulation is single: blood passes through the heart once per circuit, going heart, gills, body, heart.

The drop from 5 kPa to 3.5 kPa is the pressure lost in the gill capillaries, and in a single circulation this reduced-pressure blood goes straight on to the body without being pumped again. In the double circulation of a mammal, blood from the lungs returns to the left side of the heart and is pumped a second time, so the aorta carries blood at high pressure.

A student who believes pressure is constant around a circuit picks this. Flow through narrow capillaries always causes a large pressure drop; the fish data are exactly what a single circulation predicts.

A student who thinks artery walls pump picks this. Arterial pressure comes from the ventricle; the high aortic pressure in a mammal is because blood returning from the lungs is pumped a second time by the left ventricle in a double circulation (B3.2.14).

mcqs.q: Which sequence correctly traces deoxygenated blood from the body through the heart and back to the body?
options: Venae cavae, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary vein, lungs, pulmonary artery, left atrium, left ventricle, aorta
Vena cava, left atrium, left ventricle, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary vein, right atrium, right ventricle and aorta
Vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary vein, left atrium, left ventricle, aorta
Vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, coronary artery, cardiac muscle, coronary vein, left atrium, left ventricle, aorta
mcqs.specStatementText: The heart delivers blood under pressure (HL)
mcqs.explain: Deoxygenated blood returns in the venae cavae to the right atrium, passes through the atrioventricular valve into the right ventricle and is pumped through the semilunar valve into the pulmonary artery. Oxygenated blood from the lungs returns in the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, enters the left ventricle and leaves in the aorta.
rationales: A student who assumes the vein is the vessel that carries deoxygenated blood picks this. The pulmonary artery carries blood away from the heart to the lungs; the pulmonary vein returns oxygenated blood to the left atrium.

A student who has read the sides of the heart from the page rather than from the body picks this. Deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium and the right ventricle sends it to the lungs; the left side receives it back and pumps it to the aorta.

Deoxygenated blood returns in the venae cavae to the right atrium, passes through the atrioventricular valve into the right ventricle and is pumped through the semilunar valve into the pulmonary artery. Oxygenated blood from the lungs returns in the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, enters the left ventricle and leaves in the aorta.

A student who thinks the coronary vessels are part of the route blood takes through the heart picks this. The coronary vessels supply the heart wall itself; blood in the chambers goes to the lungs, not through the coronary circulation.

mcqs.q: The wall of the left ventricle is about three times thicker than the wall of the right ventricle. Which statement correctly explains this difference?
options: The left ventricle pumps a larger volume of blood at each beat than the right ventricle, so it needs more muscle.
The left ventricle pumps blood to the lungs, which offer more resistance to flow than the rest of the body does.
The left ventricle gets a stronger nerve impulse from the brain at each beat, so it has built up more muscle.
The left ventricle must generate a much higher pressure to drive blood through the whole systemic circulation.
mcqs.specStatementText: The heart delivers blood under pressure (HL)
mcqs.explain: This is a form-function adaptation of cardiac muscle: the thick wall of the left ventricle can develop the high pressure needed to push blood through the long, high-resistance systemic circuit, while the thinner right ventricle produces the lower pressure suited to the nearby lungs.
rationales: A student who links thickness to volume picks this. Both ventricles eject the same volume per beat; otherwise blood would accumulate in one circuit. The difference is the pressure each must generate.

A student who has reversed the two sides of the heart picks this. The left ventricle pumps to the body, and it is the systemic circulation that has the greater resistance and needs the higher pressure.

A student who thinks the brain drives each contraction picks this. The beat is initiated by the sinoatrial node in the right atrium and spreads through the heart; ventricular wall thickness reflects the pressure the chamber must generate, not the strength of any nervous input (B3.2.15).

This is a form-function adaptation of cardiac muscle: the thick wall of the left ventricle can develop the high pressure needed to push blood through the long, high-resistance systemic circuit, while the thinner right ventricle produces the lower pressure suited to the nearby lungs.

mcqs.q: The sinoatrial node fires. Which sequence of events then follows in the left side of the heart?
options: The atrium contracts, filling the ventricle; the ventricle then contracts, shutting the atrioventricular valve and opening the semilunar valve; then both relax.
The atrium and the ventricle contract at the same moment, and the atrioventricular and semilunar valves open together to let blood into the aorta.
Muscles attached to the valves pull them open one after the other, and the ventricle contracts only after both valves have been opened.
A nerve impulse from the brain reaches the ventricle first, so the ventricle contracts and then the atrium contracts to refill it.
mcqs.specStatementText: The cardiac cycle and blood pressure readings (HL)
mcqs.explain: The impulse spreads across the atria first, so atrial systole completes ventricular filling. After a brief delay the ventricle contracts: its rising pressure shuts the atrioventricular valve and, once it exceeds aortic pressure, opens the semilunar valve. Diastole follows, with both chambers relaxed and filling.
rationales: The impulse spreads across the atria first, so atrial systole completes ventricular filling. After a brief delay the ventricle contracts: its rising pressure shuts the atrioventricular valve and, once it exceeds aortic pressure, opens the semilunar valve. Diastole follows, with both chambers relaxed and filling.
A student who pictures the heart as squeezing all at once picks this. Atrial systole precedes ventricular systole, and the atrioventricular valve must be shut while the semilunar valve is open.
A student who thinks the valves are operated by muscles picks this. Valves have no muscle; they open and shut passively as the pressure differences across them change during the cycle.
A student who thinks the brain initiates each beat picks this. The beat is initiated by the sinoatrial node in the heart itself, and its impulse reaches the atria before the ventricles.

mcqs.q: A person's blood pressure is recorded as 120/80 mm Hg. Which interpretation of the two values is correct?
options: 120 is the pressure inside the left ventricle when it contracts and 80 is the pressure inside the left atrium when it relaxes.
120 is the arterial pressure at the peak of ventricular systole and 80 is the arterial pressure during ventricular diastole.
120 is the pressure during systole and 80 is the pressure the artery wall itself generates as it contracts to push blood.
120 is the pressure during systole; the true diastolic pressure is zero, and 80 is an average over the whole cycle.
mcqs.specStatementText: The cardiac cycle and blood pressure readings (HL)
mcqs.explain: Blood pressure is measured in an artery. The systolic value is the maximum pressure reached when the left ventricle contracts and forces blood into the arteries; the diastolic value is the minimum, maintained by elastic recoil of the artery walls while the ventricle relaxes and refills.
rationales: A student who assumes the reading is taken inside the heart picks this. Both values are pressures measured in an artery of the arm, not in the chambers of the heart.

Blood pressure is measured in an artery. The systolic value is the maximum pressure reached when the left ventricle contracts and forces blood into the arteries; the diastolic value is the minimum, maintained by elastic recoil of the artery walls while the ventricle relaxes and refills.
A student who thinks artery walls pump picks this. The diastolic pressure is maintained by passive elastic recoil, not by contraction of the artery wall.

A student who thinks pressure vanishes when the heart relaxes picks this. Arterial pressure never falls to zero, because the stretched elastic walls recoil and keep the blood under pressure; 80 is the actual diastolic pressure.

mcqs.q: A cut stem of a well-watered plant exudes sap from the xylem for several hours. When the roots are treated with a respiratory inhibitor, the exudation stops. What does this show about how the sap was being pushed out?
options: Root cells were actively transporting water into the xylem, and this active transport of water molecules needs ATP from respiration.
The exudation was caused by tension pulling water up the xylem, and the inhibitor stopped the transpiration that generates it.
Root cells were using ATP to pump mineral ions into the xylem, so water entered by osmosis and produced a positive pressure.
The xylem vessels themselves were using ATP from respiration to push the sap upwards, and the inhibitor stopped them.
mcqs.specStatementText: Root pressure pushes from below (HL)
mcqs.explain: Root pressure is generated by active transport of mineral ions into the xylem. This lowers the water potential of the xylem sap, water follows by osmosis, and the accumulating water produces a positive pressure potential that pushes sap up the stem. Inhibiting respiration removes the ATP for ion transport, so the pressure collapses.
rationales: A student who thinks water itself is actively transported picks this. Water is never actively transported; it is mineral ions that are pumped into the xylem, and water follows by osmosis.

A student who merges root pressure with transpiration pull picks this. A cut stem has no leaves to transpire, and tension would draw water in rather than push it out; the positive pressure was generated in the roots.

Root pressure is generated by active transport of mineral ions into the xylem. This lowers the water potential of the xylem sap, water follows by osmosis, and the accumulating water produces a positive pressure potential that pushes sap up the stem. Inhibiting respiration removes the ATP for ion transport, so the pressure collapses.

A student who thinks xylem is living and transports water actively picks this. Mature xylem vessels are dead and have no cell contents; the ATP-dependent step is the active transport of mineral ions by living root cells around the xylem (B3.2.17, B3.2.8).

mcqs.q: Droplets of water appear at the leaf tips of a grass seedling overnight, when the air is saturated with water vapour, but not during a dry, sunny day. Which explanation is correct?
options: At night the roots generate a tension that pulls water up the plant and out of the leaf tips, taking over from the pull of transpiration.
At night root cells use ATP to actively transport water molecules into the xylem, and this pumping of water forces it out of the leaf tips.
Root pressure alone can lift water up the plant at any time of day, so droplets should appear whether or not the air is humid.
Humid air stops transpiration, so root pressure generated by active ion transport pushes water up and out of the leaf tips.
mcqs.specStatementText: Root pressure pushes from below (HL)
mcqs.explain: Root pressure is generated when transport in the xylem due to transpiration is insufficient, such as when high humidity prevents transpiration. Active transport of mineral ions into the root xylem draws in water by osmosis, and the resulting positive pressure forces water up the small seedling and out at the leaf tips.
rationales: A student who thinks root pressure is a pull picks this. Root pressure is a positive pressure potential generated in the root; a tension could not force water out of a leaf.

A student who thinks water itself is actively transported picks this. Root pressure arises from active transport of mineral ions into the xylem; water follows by osmosis and is never pumped directly (B3.2.17).
A student who thinks water is always pushed up from the roots picks this. During the day the rapid loss of water by transpiration removes the water as fast as it arrives, so no excess is forced out.

Root pressure is generated when transport in the xylem due to transpiration is insufficient, such as when high humidity prevents transpiration. Active transport of mineral ions into the root xylem draws in water by osmosis, and the resulting positive pressure forces water up the small seedling and out at the leaf tips.

mcqs.q: Which feature of a sieve tube element helps sap to flow along the phloem?
options: It has lost its nucleus and most of its cytoplasm and organelles, so little inside it obstructs the sap.
It is dead and empty like a xylem vessel, so there is nothing inside the cell to slow the flow of sap.
Its end walls are solid plates that hold the sap under pressure so that it flows faster along the tube.
It contains many mitochondria, whose ATP is used to push the sap along the tube towards the sink.
mcqs.specStatementText: Phloem: sieve tubes and companion cells (HL)
mcqs.explain: Sieve tube elements are living cells adapted for flow: reduced cytoplasm, few organelles and no nucleus leave the lumen largely clear, and perforated sieve plates at the ends let sap pass to the next element. The neighbouring companion cell provides the functions the element has given up.
rationales: Sieve tube elements are living cells adapted for flow: reduced cytoplasm, few organelles and no nucleus leave the lumen largely clear, and perforated sieve plates at the ends let sap pass to the next element. The neighbouring companion cell provides the functions the element has given up.
A student who models phloem on xylem picks this. Sieve tube elements are alive, kept alive by companion cells; a dead phloem cell could not be loaded or unloaded.
A student who takes plate to mean a solid barrier picks this. Sieve plates are perforated; solid end walls would stop the flow altogether.
A student who thinks ATP propels the sap picks this. It is the companion cell that has many mitochondria, and their ATP is used for loading and unloading sugars, not for pushing sap along.

mcqs.q: In spring, sugars stored in the roots of a deciduous tree are converted to sucrose and carried in the phloem to the opening buds. Which statement about this transport is correct?
options: Mitochondria in the companion cells provide the ATP that physically drives the sap along the sieve tubes up to the buds.
Companion cells in the root use ATP to load sucrose into the sieve tubes, and the sap flows up to the buds, the sinks.
Sap cannot move upwards in the phloem, so the sugars must instead be carried up to the buds in the xylem.
The sieve tube elements must first be killed and emptied, as in xylem, before any sap is able to flow through them.
mcqs.specStatementText: Phloem: sieve tubes and companion cells (HL)
mcqs.explain: Phloem sap flows from source to sink. Here the root is the source: its companion cells, rich in mitochondria, actively load sucrose into the sieve tube elements through plasmodesmata, and the sap moves up to the buds, the sinks, where sugars are unloaded for growth.
rationales: A student who thinks ATP pushes the sap picks this. ATP from companion cells is used to load sucrose into the sieve tubes at the root and unload it at the buds; the flow along the tube is by pressure.

Phloem sap flows from source to sink. Here the root is the source: its companion cells, rich in mitochondria, actively load sucrose into the sieve tube elements through plasmodesmata, and the sap moves up to the buds, the sinks, where sugars are unloaded for growth.
A student who believes phloem sap only flows downwards picks this. Sap flows from any source to any sink, so in spring it moves upwards from the storage root to the buds.

A student who thinks sieve tube elements are dead picks this. They are living cells with reduced contents; loading sucrose requires living companion cells and sieve tube elements connected by plasmodesmata.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic B3.2 Transport

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Lymph is treated only as excess tissue fluid entering thin-walled lymph ducts through gaps, moved past valves that prevent backflow, and returned to the blood circulation via veins. No content is included on lymph nodes, lymphocytes or the immune functions of the lymphatic system, on the names of the thoracic duct or other specific vessels, or on absorption of fats by lacteals.

Single and double circulation are tested only as the sequence of organs (heart, gills, body; heart, lungs, heart, body), the number of passes through the heart per circuit, and the consequence for blood pressure reaching the body. No content is included on the chambers of the fish heart, on amphibian or reptile circulations, or on the evolutionary origin of the double circulation.

Phloem is treated only through the named adaptations and how they ease flow and support loading at sources and unloading at sinks. The pressure-flow mechanism is mentioned only qualitatively (m44, c39) to explain why ATP is spent on loading rather than on propelling sap; the symplastic and apoplastic loading pathways and the biochemistry of sucrose transporters are not included, so nothing in the bank rests on content reported as removed in the 2028 revision.

omitted.sequence: no authored ordering; would require inventing a sequence
